title: "8 · Quantum information protocols"
code-tools: false

![](../assets/thumbs/ch08.png){width=60% fig-align=center fig-alt="Quantum information protocols"}

A quantum information protocol is a recipe for parties in separate laboratories. By convention the sender is Alice and
the receiver is Bob; a third party, Charlie, may sit between them as the source of entangled pairs or as a relay. The
protocol is the complete list of instructions: who prepares which state, who measures what, and who sends which message
to whom and when. It is judged by what arrives, for example how many bits reach Bob, or how close his final state is to
the one Alice intended.

Three kinds of resource can connect the laboratories. Classical bits travel over an ordinary channel, a telephone line
in the standard picture. Qubits travel over a quantum channel, for example as photons in an optical fibre. And the
parties may share entangled pairs distributed in advance; one shared Bell pair $(\vert00\rangle+\vert11\rangle)/\sqrt2$
is called one **ebit**. When no qubit may cross between the laboratories, each party can still apply gates and
measurements to its own qubits and adapt them to what it hears on the telephone. This class of operations is called
local operations and classical communication (LOCC). LOCC cannot create entanglement and can only use it up, so shared
pairs are a resource that protocols consume.

Quantum mechanics imposes rules with no classical counterpart. An unknown quantum state cannot be copied (the no-cloning
theorem, notebook 20). A measurement of one qubit returns a single bit and disturbs the state, so one copy of an unknown
state cannot be read out (notebooks 20 and 23). Entangled pairs produce correlations stronger than any classical
mechanism allows (notebook 19), yet they carry no signal: nothing Alice does to her qubit changes the statistics of Bob's
until a classical message arrives (notebooks 20 and 21). The disturbance caused by measurement also lets Alice and Bob
detect an eavesdropper, conventionally called Eve; that use, quantum key distribution, belongs to a later chapter on
quantum communication and cryptography.

The notebooks build on each other. Notebook 19 introduces the four Bell states and the CHSH inequality, which shows that
the correlations of an entangled pair exceed those of any classical model. Notebook 20 teleports an unknown qubit state
with one ebit and two classical bits. Notebook 21 treats entanglement as a currency: entanglement swapping joins two short
entangled links into one long link, as a quantum repeater does, and superdense coding spends one ebit to carry two
classical bits on one qubit. Notebook 22 moves from two qubits to $N$ with the GHZ state, certifies its entanglement and
follows how local noise destroys it faster as $N$ grows. Every protocol is simulated shot by shot, with mid-circuit
measurements and classical feed-forward where the protocol needs them, and then exposed to noise.

The last two notebooks reverse the question and ask which state a device has actually produced. Notebook 23
reconstructs the full density matrix from measurement counts (quantum state tomography) by linear inversion, least
squares and maximum likelihood. Notebook 24 uses classical shadows, randomised measurements that predict many
observables without reconstructing the state.

## Notebooks in this chapter

::: {.nb-item}
[Bell states and the CHSH inequality — violation of local realism in simulated measurements](../ch08_quantum_information_protocols/19_bell_states_and_chsh.ipynb)

The four Bell states and the circuit that makes them, their correlations and maximally mixed marginals, a full derivation of the local-hidden-variable bound |S| <= 2 and of Tsirelson's bound 2*sqrt(2), a simulated shot-by-shot CHSH experiment with error bars, and the fate of the violation under white noise, dephasing and imperfect detectors.
:::

::: {.nb-item}
[Quantum teleportation — no-cloning, Bell measurement and classical feed-forward](../ch08_quantum_information_protocols/20_quantum_teleportation.ipynb)

A complete derivation and simulation of quantum teleportation: the no-cloning theorem with proof, the Bell-basis algebra of the protocol, a jit/vmap-compatible mid-circuit measurement with classical feed-forward, uniform outcome statistics and no-signalling, the classical 2/3 benchmark derived from a Haar-averaging identity, teleportation through a noisy Bell pair on the density tensor and via trajectories, and the deferred-measurement circuit.
:::

::: {.nb-item}
[Entanglement swapping and superdense coding](../ch08_quantum_information_protocols/21_entanglement_swapping_and_superdense_coding.ipynb)

Two protocols that turn entanglement into a resource: swapping entanglement between particles that never met (with the complete four-qubit algebra, mid-circuit Bell measurement, feed-forward, noisy Werner links and the repeater chain), and sending two classical bits down one qubit, with decoding statistics, the Holevo bound, and the rate and capacity of a noisy shared pair.
:::

::: {.nb-item}
[GHZ states and decoherence — genuine multipartite entanglement and its fragility](../ch08_quantum_information_protocols/22_ghz_states_and_decoherence.ipynb)

Building N-qubit GHZ states with a CNOT cascade and with a log-depth tree, certifying them through stabilisers, parity oscillations and the fidelity witness, and then watching local dephasing, depolarising and amplitude damping destroy them — analytically, on the density tensor, and with quantum trajectories up to twelve qubits.
:::

::: {.nb-item}
[Quantum state tomography — linear inversion, least squares and maximum likelihood](../ch08_quantum_information_protocols/23_quantum_state_tomography.ipynb)

How to reconstruct an unknown density matrix from measured click statistics: the Pauli/Bloch linear model and its design matrix, ordinary and weighted least squares with error propagation, the unphysical-estimate problem and its projection fix, the RρR and gradient-based maximum-likelihood estimators, and an accuracy-versus-shots assessment up to four qubits.
:::

::: {.nb-item}
[Classical shadows — tomography without the $4^N$ wall](../ch08_quantum_information_protocols/24_classical_shadows.ipynb)

Randomised measurements turned into an unbiased classical description of a quantum state: the measurement channel and its inverse derived for random Pauli bases and for global Clifford ensembles, the single-snapshot estimator and its variance (the shadow norm), median of means, and many observables — correlators, an energy, a fidelity, a reconstructed density matrix — predicted from one data set.
:::
